name: Spanish Essentials
author: Recurse
subject: languages
description: Greetings, ser vs estar, articles, present-tense verbs, numbers and question words.

lesson.intro: Spanish is an official language in about 20 countries across Spain and Latin America. This pack gives you the core of a first conversation: greeting people, saying who you are and how you feel, naming things, and using the most common verbs in the present tense.

sections.title: Greetings and introductions
sections.body:
Spanish greetings change with the time of day:

- Buenos días: good morning, until lunch (around 1 or 2 p.m.)
- Buenas tardes: good afternoon, until it gets dark
- Buenas noches: good evening or good night, also used to say goodbye
- Hola: hi, at any time of day

Spanish has two ways to say "you". Use tú with friends, family, children and people your age in casual settings. Use usted with strangers, older people and in formal situations. Usted takes the same verb form as él (he) and ella (she): ¿Cómo estás? (to a friend) becomes ¿Cómo está usted? (to a stranger).

Written questions and exclamations open with an upside-down mark: ¿Cómo estás? ¡Hola!

Courtesy words you will use every day: por favor (please), gracias (thank you), de nada (you're welcome), perdón (sorry, excuse me), adiós (goodbye), hasta luego (see you later).
sections.code:
A: ¡Hola! ¿Cómo te llamas?
B: Me llamo Lucía. ¿Y tú?
A: Me llamo Tom. Mucho gusto.
B: Igualmente. ¿Cómo estás?
A: Bien, gracias.
sections.tip: Me llamo literally means "I call myself". Soy Lucía (I am Lucía) works too.

check.question: It is 4 p.m. and you walk into a shop. Which greeting fits best?
check.explanation: Buenas tardes covers the afternoon until dark. Buenos días is for the morning, and buenas días is wrong because día is masculine.

sections.title: Ser and estar: two verbs for "to be"
sections.body:
Spanish has two verbs that mean "to be", and they are not interchangeable.

Use ser for what something is: identity, origin, profession, nationality, lasting traits and time.

- Soy Ana. (identity)
- Es de Chile. (origin: ser + de)
- Mi padre es profesor. (profession, with no article before the job)
- Son las tres. (time: it is three o'clock)

Use estar for where something is and how it is right now: location, feelings and temporary conditions.

- Estoy en casa. (location)
- Estamos cansados. (condition: we are tired)
- ¿Cómo estás? (how you feel)

Some adjectives change meaning with the verb: Juan es aburrido means Juan is boring (a trait), while Juan está aburrido means Juan is bored (right now).
sections.code:
ser     estar
yo                      soy     estoy
tú                      eres    estás
él, ella, usted         es      está
nosotros                somos   estamos
vosotros                sois    estáis
ellos, ellas, ustedes   son     están
sections.tip: The location of an event is an exception: La fiesta es en mi casa (the party is at my house) uses ser.

check.question: Which verb completes the sentence? Las llaves ___ en la mesa. (The keys are on the table.)
check.explanation: This is location, so it takes estar, and las llaves is plural, so the form is están. Son is the tempting choice, but ser does not describe where things are.

sections.title: Articles, gender and plurals
sections.body:
Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, and the words around it must match. El and la mean "the"; un and una mean "a". In the plural they become los, las, unos and unas.

Nouns ending in -o are usually masculine and nouns ending in -a are usually feminine, but common exceptions exist: el día (day), el mapa (map), el problema (problem), la mano (hand). Learn every noun together with its article.

To make a noun plural:

- After a vowel, add -s: casa → casas
- After a consonant, add -es: ciudad → ciudades
- A final -z becomes -ces: lápiz → lápices

Adjectives usually come after the noun and match it in gender and number: el libro rojo, la casa roja, los libros rojos, las casas rojas. Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant change only for number: un chico inteligente, una chica inteligente. A group that mixes masculine and feminine uses the masculine plural, so los niños can mean boys, or boys and girls together.
sections.code:
singular             plural
masculine   el libro, un libro   los libros, unos libros
feminine    la mesa, una mesa    las mesas, unas mesas

check.question: What is the plural of la ciudad (the city)?
check.explanation: Ciudad ends in a consonant, so it adds -es, and the feminine article la becomes las: las ciudades.

sections.title: Present tense: regular verbs and tener, ir, hacer
sections.body:
The dictionary form of a verb (the infinitive) ends in -ar, -er or -ir. To conjugate a regular verb, drop that ending and add the ending for the person, as in the table below.

Because the ending already shows who is acting, the subject pronoun is usually left out: Hablo español means I speak Spanish.

Three very common verbs are irregular and must be memorized:

- tener (to have): tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen. Spanish uses tener for age: Tengo veinte años (I am twenty, literally I have twenty years).
- ir (to go): voy, vas, va, vamos, vais, van. Ir a + infinitive talks about the near future: Voy a comer (I am going to eat).
- hacer (to do, to make): hago, haces, hace, hacemos, hacéis, hacen. Weather uses hace: Hace frío (it is cold), Hace calor (it is hot).
sections.code:
hablar     comer     vivir
yo                      hablo      como      vivo
tú                      hablas     comes     vives
él, ella, usted         habla      come      vive
nosotros                hablamos   comemos   vivimos
vosotros                habláis    coméis    vivís
ellos, ellas, ustedes   hablan     comen     viven
sections.tip: Vosotros (you all, informal) is used only in Spain. In Latin America, ustedes is used for every group.

check.question: Which form completes the sentence? Ellos ___ pan todos los días. (comer, to eat)
check.explanation: For -er verbs the ellos ending is -en, so comer becomes comen. Coman is the mistake of using the -an ending that belongs to -ar verbs.

sections.title: Numbers and question words
sections.body:
Numbers 0 to 15 have their own names: cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez, once, doce, trece, catorce, quince.

From 16 to 29 they are written as one word: dieciséis (16), diecisiete (17), dieciocho (18), diecinueve (19), veinte (20), veintiuno (21), veintidós (22), veintitrés (23). From 31 on, the tens and units are joined with y: treinta y uno (31), cuarenta y cinco (45). The tens are treinta, cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta, noventa, and 100 is cien.

Question words carry a written accent:

- ¿Qué? what
- ¿Quién? who
- ¿Dónde? where
- ¿Cuándo? when
- ¿Por qué? why (the answer porque, because, is one word with no accent)
- ¿Cómo? how
- ¿Cuánto? how much, how many
- ¿Cuál? which
sections.code:
¿Dónde vives? Vivo en Lima.
¿Cuántos años tienes? Tengo treinta y dos años.
¿Qué hora es? Son las tres.
sections.tip: Uno becomes un before a masculine noun: un libro, veintiún años.

check.question: Which question word asks "when?"
check.explanation: ¿Cuándo? means when. It is easy to confuse with ¿Cuánto? (how much), which differs by one letter.

keyTerms.definition: The two words for "you": tú is informal (friends, family, children); usted is formal (strangers, elders, work) and takes the él/ella verb form.
"To be" for what something is: identity, origin, profession, lasting traits and time (soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son).
"To be" for where something is and how it is right now: location, feelings, conditions (estoy, estás, está, estamos, estáis, están).
Every noun is masculine or feminine, and its articles and adjectives must match: el libro, la mesa.
Articles and adjectives change to match the noun in gender and number: las casas rojas.
The dictionary form of a verb, ending in -ar, -er or -ir: hablar, comer, vivir.
The everyday way to talk about the near future: Voy a comer (I am going to eat).

summary: Greet by time of day (buenos días, buenas tardes, buenas noches); use usted with strangers and tú with friends.
Ser says what something is; estar says where it is and how it is right now.
Articles and adjectives match the noun in gender and number: las casas rojas.
Regular verbs drop -ar, -er or -ir and add a person ending; tener, ir and hacer are irregular and must be memorized.
Question words carry an accent (dónde, cuándo, cuánto), and written questions open with ¿.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain when to use ser and when to use estar to a friend starting Spanish, with one example sentence for each.

questions.question: Translate into Spanish: Good morning.
questions.explanation: Buenos días is the standard morning greeting, used until around lunchtime. Día is masculine, so it is buenos, not buenas. Buen día is also common in parts of Latin America.

questions.question: Translate into Spanish, speaking to a friend: How are you?
questions.explanation: ¿Cómo estás? uses the tú form of estar, which suits a friend. With a stranger you would say ¿Cómo está usted? ¿Qué tal? is a casual alternative.

questions.question: How do you politely ask a stranger's name in Spanish?
questions.answer: ¿Cómo se llama usted? Usted is the formal "you" for strangers and older people; with a friend, ask ¿Cómo te llamas?
questions.explanation: Both questions use llamarse (to be called): the formal one uses se with the usted form, the informal one uses te with the tú form. Answer with Me llamo ... (My name is ...).

questions.question: Choose the right verb: Mi hermana ___ médica. (My sister is a doctor.)
questions.explanation: Professions use ser because they say what someone is, and es is the form for ella. Está would describe where she is or how she feels, not her job.

questions.question: Choose the right verb: Madrid ___ en España.
questions.explanation: Location uses estar, and Madrid takes the third-person singular form está. Es is the common mistake: ser says what something is, not where it is.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'Juan es aburrido' and 'Juan está aburrido'?
choices: They mean the same; está is just more formal
Es aburrido means he is bored now; está aburrido means he is boring
Es aburrido means he is boring; está aburrido means he is bored now
Está aburrido is wrong; aburrido only works with ser
questions.explanation: Ser gives a lasting trait (he is a boring person) and estar gives a current state (he is bored at the moment). Swapping the two meanings is the usual mix-up: estar is for how someone is right now.

questions.question: Translate into Spanish: I am from Mexico.
questions.explanation: Origin uses ser + de: soy de México. The pronoun yo is optional because soy already means "I am". Estoy de México is wrong because estar is not used for origin.

questions.question: Which phrase correctly says 'the red houses'?
questions.explanation: Casa is feminine, so the plural article is las and the adjective takes the feminine plural ending -as. Las casas rojos is the common slip: the adjective must match the noun too, not only the article.

questions.question: Which of these nouns takes el, even though it ends in -a?
questions.explanation: Día is masculine: el día, buenos días. Mesa, casa and semana follow the usual pattern and are feminine (la mesa, la casa, la semana). El mapa and el problema are other masculine nouns ending in -a.

questions.question: Make 'el lápiz' (the pencil) plural.
questions.explanation: A final -z changes to -c before -es is added, and el becomes los: los lápices. Lápizes is a common spelling mistake.

questions.question: Conjugate hablar (to speak) for yo.
questions.explanation: Drop -ar to get the stem habl- and add the yo ending -o: hablo. Hablas is the tú form and habla is the form for él or ella.

questions.question: Complete with escribir (to write): Tú ___ una carta.
questions.explanation: Escribir is a regular -ir verb, and the tú ending for -er and -ir verbs is -es: escribes. Escribís is the vosotros form, escribe is for él or ella, and escribas wrongly uses the -as ending of -ar verbs.

questions.question: Translate into Spanish: I am twenty years old.
questions.explanation: Spanish states age with tener: literally "I have twenty years". Soy veinte años is a common mistake copied from English. Write años with ñ if you can, since anos is a different word.

questions.question: Translate into Spanish: I am going to eat.
questions.explanation: Ir a + infinitive expresses the near future: voy (I go) + a + comer. Only ir is conjugated; voy a como is wrong because the second verb stays in the infinitive.

questions.question: How do you say 'It is cold' about the weather in Spanish?
questions.answer: Hace frío. Weather uses hacer (literally "it makes cold"). For a person who feels cold, use tener: Tengo frío.
questions.explanation: Spanish describes weather with hace: hace frío, hace calor, hace sol. Está frío describes a thing, such as cold coffee (el café está frío), not the weather.

questions.question: Write the number 23 in Spanish words.
questions.explanation: Numbers from 21 to 29 are single words: veinti- plus the unit, so veintiuno, veintidós, veintitrés. From 31 on, the tens and units are joined with y (treinta y tres).

questions.question: Translate the question word into Spanish: where?
questions.explanation: ¿Dónde? asks about place, as in ¿Dónde vives? (Where do you live?). Question words carry a written accent; donde without one is used in statements, as in la casa donde vivo.

questions.question: How do you ask 'How much does it cost?' in Spanish?
questions.answer: ¿Cuánto cuesta? For more than one item, ask ¿Cuánto cuestan?
questions.explanation: Cuánto means how much, and cuesta is the él/ella form of costar (to cost). It is one of the most useful phrases for shopping and travel.
